title: safe_globals default path returns ns['__builtins__'] aliasing the shared module-global _SAFE_BUILTINS; mutation leaks across all subsequent exec namespaces (inconsistent with the allow_imports branch)
description: _SAFE_BUILTINS is a module-global dict whose '__builtins__' key is set to itself at line 109. In safe_globals, the default (allow_imports=False) path does `ns = dict(_SAFE_BUILTINS)` (a shallow copy of the entries) but the copied '__builtins__' value still points at the original _SAFE_BUILTINS object. So ns['__builtins__'] IS the shared module-global, not a per-call copy. Any mutation through ns['__builtins__'] (e.g. side effects of exec that add/remove a builtins entry, or any code path that writes through the builtins mapping) permanently corrupts _SAFE_BUILTINS for every subsequent exec() in the entire process. This is a shared-mutable-state hazard and a contract violation for a function whose purpose is to hand back an isolated namespace. It is also internally inconsistent: the allow_imports=True branch (line 125) deliberately builds a FRESH dict `{**_SAFE_BUILTINS, '__import__': ...}` for ns['__builtins__'], so the two branches have asymmetric isolation guarantees for no stated reason.
evidence: Executed: `g = safe_globals(pl=...)`; `g['__builtins__'] is _SAFE_BUILTINS` -> True. `g['__builtins__']['LEAKED'] = 'pwned'` then `'LEAKED' in _SAFE_BUILTINS` -> True, and a fresh `safe_globals()` call sees 'LEAKED' at both top level and under '__builtins__'. The AST validator currently blocks direct `__builtins__[...]=` in user code, but safe_globals is a public reusable helper (used by executor and preamble) whose isolation contract is violated and whose two branches disagree.
